content_units: Ontario Deposit Dispute Snapshot

In Ontario, a landlord generally   cannot keep a damage deposit for scuffs or wear   because residential damage deposits are not permitted under the Residential Tenancies Act; landlords can usually collect only a   last month’s rent deposit   and certain lawful key deposits. For a move-out on   2025-08-31  , wall scuffs and ordinary carpet wear after a one-year tenancy are often treated as   normal wear and tear  , not tenant-chargeable damage.
Tenant Options and Evidence Checklist
Context for this situation
- Lease start:   2024-09-01
- No pets, no smoking
- Move-in photos already show   some prior wear
- Claimed deduction:   CAD 900   for wall scuffs and carpet wear
What the tenant can do now
Option 1:   Request return of the withheld amount in writing     Best first step if the deduction was informal or unsupported   Fast, low-cost
Send demand
Option 2:   Ask for an itemized breakdown and proof     Request invoices, photos, inspection notes, and explanation of why damage exceeds normal wear   Strengthens negotiation
Learn evidence
Option 3:   File an application with the Landlord and Tenant Board     Appropriate if the landlord refuses repayment   Formal remedy path
LTB forms
Option 4:   Use a community legal clinic or tenant duty counsel     Good if the landlord is aggressive or the facts are disputed   Helpful for drafting and strategy
Find legal help
Documents to gather
- Lease agreement
- Receipt or proof of the   deposit paid
- Move-in photos/videos showing existing wear
- Move-out photos/videos showing final condition
- Emails, texts, or letters with the landlord
- Any move-in or move-out inspection reports
- Proof of professional cleaning, if any
- Witness statements from roommates, cleaners, or movers
- The landlord’s deduction notice, invoice, or explanation
- Proof no pets/no smoking applied during the tenancy
What usually counts as normal wear and tear
- Light wall scuffs or minor marks from ordinary use
- Small nail holes or minor picture-hook marks
- Carpet flattening from walking
- Mild carpet shading or ordinary aging
- Faded paint from sunlight or time
- Loose door handles or minor hardware wear from normal use
What may be beyond normal wear and tear
- Large holes in walls
- Deep gouges, deliberate markings, or extensive repainting caused by misuse
- Carpet burns, heavy staining, strong pet odours, or tears
- Broken fixtures caused by impact or neglect
- Water damage caused by tenant conduct
- Missing landlord-provided items
Why this tenant may have a stronger position
- One-year occupancy is consistent with   ordinary use
- No pets and no smoking reduce common damage arguments
- Move-in photos showing   pre-existing wear   can undermine the landlord’s claim
- “Wall scuffs” and “carpet wear” are often classic wear-and-tear issues unless unusually severe
Concise Dispute Letter Template
Subject: Request for Return of Wrongfully Withheld Deposit Funds
Dear [Landlord Name],
I am writing regarding the   CAD 900   withheld after my tenancy ended on   2025-08-31   for alleged wall scuffs and carpet wear.

I dispute this deduction. My tenancy ran from   2024-09-01 to 2025-08-31  , and the unit was left in ordinary lived-in condition. The move-in photos show some prior wear already existed, and there were   no pets   and   no smoking   during my tenancy. The issues described appear to be normal wear and tear rather than tenant-caused damage.
Please return the withheld   CAD 900   by   [insert date, e.g., 7 days from sending]  . If you believe the deduction is valid, please provide:
- an itemized statement of the charges,
- dated before-and-after photos,
- receipts or repair invoices, and
- an explanation of why the condition exceeds normal wear and tear.
If the amount is not returned, I will consider pursuing my remedies through the appropriate Ontario housing dispute process.
Sincerely,
[Tenant Name]
[Current Address]
[Phone / Email]
